hook: Vinegar is about 0.8 M acetic acid, yet you can splash it on a salad. A hydrochloric acid solution of the same concentration would have a pH near 0. The difference is that most acetic acid molecules never give up their proton: the reaction reaches equilibrium with the acid mostly intact.

prereq.q: For A ⇌ 2 B with K = 4.0 × 10⁻⁶ and [A]₀ = 0.10 M, what does the small-x approximation replace (0.10 − x) with?
prereq.why: When K is small, x is tiny compared with 0.10, so 0.10 − x ≈ 0.10. You check afterwards that x is under 5% of 0.10.

prereq.q: What is the pH of 0.010 M HCl?
What is the conjugate base of HNO₂?
prereq.why: Remove one H⁺ from the acid: HNO₂ → NO₂⁻.

figure.caption: The same amount of acid: the strong acid is all ions, the weak acid mostly whole molecules.

chain.cause: A weak acid holds its proton fairly tightly
chain.effect: HA + H₂O ⇌ H₃O⁺ + A⁻ reaches equilibrium with most HA un-ionized (Ka ≪ 1)

chain.cause: Only a small amount x ionizes
chain.effect: an ICE table gives Ka = x²/(C − x) ≈ x²/C, so [H₃O⁺] ≈ √(Ka·C)
Q falls below Ka, so a larger fraction ionizes: percent ionization rises

chain.cause: An acid and its conjugate base are linked through water
chain.effect: Ka × Kb = Kw, so the weaker the acid, the stronger its conjugate base

ideas: Weak acid: Ka ≪ 1, mostly un-ionized. Larger Ka (smaller pKa) = stronger acid.
Weak acid pH: [H₃O⁺] = x ≈ √(Ka × C). Check x < 5% of C; if not, solve the quadratic.
Weak base: same method with Kb to find [OH⁻], then pOH, then pH.
Ka × Kb = Kw for a conjugate pair; pKa + pKb = 14.00 at 25 °C. Kb is not 1/Ka.

misconception.wrong: A weak acid is one that is dilute.
misconception.right: Weak means it ionizes only partly (Ka ≪ 1); dilute means low concentration. Concentrated acetic acid is still weak, and 0.0010 M HCl is still strong.

summary: A weak acid or base reacts with water only partly, so its pH comes from an equilibrium. With Ka (or Kb) and the concentration, an ICE table and the small-x approximation give [H₃O⁺] ≈ √(Ka·C). Percent ionization rises on dilution, and a conjugate pair obeys Ka × Kb = Kw.
